summary: Defines extensions to the Link Management Protocol so it can be used between a peer node and an adjacent optical line system. They are meant to meet the Optical Link Interface Requirements. It is a standards-track document.

plainLanguage.summary: Network devices need to talk to the long-distance optical equipment attached to them. This memo gives them a shared language.

what is a link group id in lmp
how does lmp work with dwdm
subtitle: Letting optical routers and switches ask the DWDM line equipment between them about link health and properties.

tldr.problem: Optical line systems (OLSes) know the configuration and state of the long-haul DWDM link between two peer nodes, but the Link Management Protocol (LMP) only worked between peer nodes themselves.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC extends LMP so a peer node can run a session with an adjacent OLS, adding a CONFIG object to tell the two kinds of session apart, six new Data Link sub-objects describing link characteristics, and a Link Group status object for fault reports.
tldr.outcome: Peer nodes get link properties and fault information from the OLS with less manual configuration. The extensions target opaque OLSes; fully transparent wavelength routing is left for later work. A later RFC 6898 updates this one.

today: RFC 4209 is a Proposed Standard from October 2005 and is updated by RFC 6898. The text itself describes only opaque line systems.

sections.title: Why Talk to the Line System
sections.content:
Networks of routers, switches, optical cross-connects (OXCs) and DWDM optical line systems (OLSes) can share a common control plane such as Generalized MPLS (GMPLS). The Link Management Protocol (LMP) manages traffic engineering (TE) links, but in its original form it only runs between peer nodes, meaning nodes that peer in signaling or routing.

The OLSes at each end of a DWDM link know how the link is configured and what state it is in. The peer nodes know the state of the label switched paths (LSPs) using the link. RFC 4209 lets the two sides share that knowledge over LMP. This reduces manual configuration and improves fault detection and recovery, and the administrative state of an LSP can be used to suppress spurious alarms from the OLS.

A peer node keeps its peer-to-OLS sessions and its peer-to-peer sessions independently. Sessions MUST be able to come up in any order, including a peer-to-peer session coming up with no peer-to-OLS session, and the reverse.
sections.plainLanguage: The equipment in the middle knows a lot about the long link, and the devices at the ends know about the traffic. They now trade notes so both sides know more.

sections.title: Scope: Opaque Line Systems
sections.content:
The extensions are meant for opaque OLSes, which examine or modify some aspect of the signal as they forward it. The document is intended for OLSes with SONET, SDH and Ethernet user ports.

Fully transparent wavelength routing was still being worked on, and the RFC says it was premature to decide what information should be exchanged there. It does provide a framework in which additional information could be exchanged later.
sections.plainLanguage: This memo covers line equipment that looks at the signal as it passes. Equipment that never looks at it is a puzzle for another day.

sections.title: Control Channel and the LMP-WDM CONFIG Object
sections.content:
LMP has four procedures: control channel management and link property correlation (mandatory), and link verification and fault management (optional). All four are supported in LMP-WDM. The RFC does not fix how the control channel is built; it could be a separate wavelength, a fiber, an Ethernet link, an IP tunnel or the overhead bytes of a data link.

Control channel management follows RFC 4204. To tell a peer-to-OLS session from a peer-to-peer session, a new LMP-WDM_CONFIG object is defined (Class 6, C-Type 2). It has a WDM bit, which indicates support for these extensions, and an OLS bit, which says whether the sender is an OLS (set) or a peer node (clear). The rest is reserved.

A node that does not support LMP-WDM MUST reply to the Config message with ConfigNack. So must a peer node configured for LMP-WDM that receives a Config message with the OLS bit clear. This catches sessions configured between the wrong kinds of device.
sections.plainLanguage: When two devices start talking, each says whether it is an end device or line equipment. If the pairing is wrong, they politely say no.

sections.title: Link Verification and Link Summarization
sections.content:
Link verification uses the Test procedure from RFC 4204. The VerifyTransportMechanism lets nodes agree on a method and matters for line systems that only see overhead bytes. For SONET or SDH user ports, the trace monitoring function of RFC 4207 may also be used.

The data links between two peer nodes are really a chain: peer to OLS, the DWDM span, and OLS to peer. When the peer-to-peer links are verified, the two OLSes must make themselves transparent. The peer nodes are responsible for coordinating this and for knowing the mapping between the two kinds of data link.

Link summarization uses the LinkSummary message to synchronize Interface_Ids and correlate link properties. It carries DATA_LINK objects made of variable-length Data Link sub-objects. A sub-object has an 8-bit Type and an 8-bit Length, and the Length MUST be at least 4 and a multiple of 4. This RFC adds six new sub-objects, chosen as properties a constraint-based path selection step would need.
sections.plainLanguage: To test the long link, the middle equipment must step aside so the end devices can check the whole path. The end devices arrange this and remember which pieces make up which path.

sections.title: The Six New Link Sub-objects
sections.content:
Each sub-object describes one data link or its DWDM span:

  • Link Group ID (Type 3, Length 8): a local ID for a group of data links, such as all links on one laser or fiber. One failure of the group can be reported in a single message. A data link can belong to several groups. 0xFFFFFFFF is reserved for all data links in a TE link, and every link is in it by default.
  • SRLG (Type 4, Length (N+1)*4): the shared risk link groups of the link, for diverse path computation. List as many as apply.
  • BER Estimate (Type 5, Length 4): an 8-bit exponent X where the bit error rate is 10 to the minus X.
  • Optical Protection (Type 6, Length 4): 6 link flags saying whether the OLS protects the link, encoded as in Section 7 of RFC 3471.
  • Total Span Length (Type 7, Length 8): the fiber length in meters, as a 32-bit unsigned integer. It may serve as a routing metric or delay estimate.
  • Administrative Group (Color) (Type 8, Length 8): a 32-bit value defined in RFC 3630.

Reserved fields are sent as zero and ignored on receipt.
sections.plainLanguage: Each sub-object is like a label on a pipe: which group it is in, how clean the signal is, whether there is a backup, and how long it is.

sections.title: Fault Management and Group Status
sections.content:
Fault management has three functions: detection, localization and notification. Detection is up to each node and is not specified. The OLS must translate failures such as excessive BER, loss of signal or SONET/SDH errors into OK, Signal Failure or Signal Degrade. It reports them with the ChannelStatus, ChannelStatusAck, ChannelStatusRequest and ChannelStatusResponse messages from RFC 4204, which can trigger peer-to-peer fault localization or GMPLS procedures directly. The OLS reports but does not take part in that localization. It may run its own localization, for example pinpointing an amplifier in a span thousands of kilometers long.

The new LINK_GROUP CHANNEL_STATUS object (Class 13, C-Type 4) pairs a 32-bit Link Group ID with a Channel Status value. It can replace the per-link CHANNEL_STATUS objects in a ChannelStatus message, so a single message covers every link in the group. The object is non-negotiable.
sections.plainLanguage: If a laser breaks, the line equipment sends one message saying everything on that laser is down, instead of one message per cable.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
LMP message security uses IPsec, as described in RFC 4204. This document only defines new objects carried in existing LMP messages, so it adds no new security considerations.

IANA assignments are made in the LMP namespaces: C-Type 2 under CONFIG (LMP-WDM_CONFIG), C-Type 4 under CHANNEL_STATUS (LINK_GROUP), and DATA_LINK sub-object Types 3 to 8.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages are protected the same way as in the base protocol, so nothing new needs guarding.
